title: A Danish view of the Milky Way
caption: The Milky Way over the Danish 1.54-meter telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way, with its bright central region, stretches over the Danish 1.54-meter telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory, lighting up the Chilean desert sky. The telescope has been at work since 1979, uncovering details about our home galaxy.

It was used for a survey lasting 15 years, published in 2004, that studied 14,000 stars in our galaxy. The project measured the stars' motions and distances, along with their ages and chemical make-up. From these, astronomers built a historical map of the Milky Way.

That map showed a far more complicated past than anyone had expected. The galaxy looks calm in this photo, but the survey found traces of a turbulent and violent history. In particular, collisions with smaller galaxies brought in huge gas clouds that set off bursts of star formation and supernova explosions, events that helped shape the galaxy we live in today.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so the Milky Way and faint stars appear brighter and richer than they would to someone standing there.

explore: The survey gave the first clues to this restless history. By combining where stars are, how they move, how old they are and what they are made of, astronomers could read the Milky Way's past much as geologists read layers of rock.
alt: The bright band and central bulge of the Milky Way stretch across a night sky above a telescope in the desert.
